name: Umayyad Emirate and Caliphate of Córdoba
summary: Muslim Spain (al-Andalus) under a branch of the Umayyad family that fled Damascus; Abd al-Rahman III made it a caliphate in 929, and Córdoba became one of the largest and most learned cities in Europe before the state broke into taifa kingdoms in 1031.

knownFor.label: Translation of learning
knownFor.note: Greek and Arabic science reached Europe.

location.value: Most of the Iberian Peninsula, centred on Córdoba, with the northern Christian kingdoms to the north.

terrain.value: Plateaus, river valleys such as the Guadalquivir, and mountains.

climate.value: Mediterranean, with hot summers and mild winters.

resources.value: Irrigated farmland, silk, olive oil, wine and metals.

disasters.value: Droughts and occasional famines hit the region.

population.value: Córdoba most likely passed 100,000 in the 10th century; one estimate gives about 450,000 around 1000.

urbanisation.value: Córdoba (perhaps 100,000 or more people in the 900s), Seville and Toledo were among the largest cities in Europe.

disease.value: Plague outbreaks, above all the Black Death (1347–51).

migration.value: Arab and Berber settlers came after the conquest of 711, and enslaved people from the north were also brought.

economicBase.value: Irrigated farming (new crops like rice, citrus), crafts.

tradeRoutes.value: Mediterranean and North African trade carried goods such as silk, spices and paper.

wealth.value: One of the richest states in Europe, based on trade, farming and taxes.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold and silver coins were minted in the 10th century; revenue was counted in dinars.

inequality.value: Jews and Christians paid a special tax called the jizya.

governmentType.value: An emirate under the Umayyad dynasty, then a caliphate from 929.

keyRulers.value: Abd al-Rahman I (independent emir from 756). Abd al-Rahman III (took the title of caliph in 929). Al-Mansur.

institutions.value: Viziers, a strong army and a court bureaucracy.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between Arabs, Berbers and the slave soldiers (saqaliba).

territoryChange.value: Christian kingdoms advanced in the north.

alliancesRivals.value: A rival of the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad and the Fatimids in North Africa.

inventions.value: Abbas ibn Firnas, a polymath who brought scientific knowledge from the east.

openness.value: Open to scholars of all faiths (with limits).

communicationTransport.value: Roman roads and rivers, along with a regular postal service.

religion.value: Muslim rulers; Christian and Jewish communities.

languageWriting.value: Arabic, with Mozarabic (Romance) and Hebrew also used.

artsArchitecture.value: Horseshoe arches, including on the Great Mosque of Córdoba.

sharedIdentity.value: An Andalusi identity blended Arab, Berber, Iberian and Jewish cultures.

dailyLife.value: Town life included baths, markets and gardens, and the farm economy used irrigation.

ideasReligions.value: Convivencia, a degree of coexistence among Muslims, Christians and Jews, supported learning and translation.

colonisation.value: Full-scale Umayyad conquest began in April 711.

riseSignals.value: Abd al-Rahman I becomes an independent emir (756).

peakPeriod.value: Caliphate (from 929), when Abd al-Rahman III took the title of caliph.

declineSignals.value: The fitna of al-Andalus begins in 1009 with the death of Abd al-Rahman Sanchuelo.

outcome.value: The caliphate crumbled in 1031 into independent taifa kingdoms.

overallCertainty.value: Main events are known from chronicles and charters; population figures are estimates.
